heart_rate.title: Heart rate
heart_rate.howToMeasure: Heart rate can be measured using a heart rate monitor, wearable sensor, ECG device, or medical monitor.
heart_rate.whyItMatters: Heart rate is a key indicator of cardiovascular function and overall physiological state. Changes in heart rate may reflect stress, physical strain, illness, or cardiovascular adaptation.
heart_rate.spaceRisk: In weightlessness, body fluids shift toward the upper body, changing the workload of the heart and blood vessels. These cardiovascular adaptations can affect heart rate regulation during long-duration missions.
heart_rate.whenToWorry: Heart rate outside the normal range may indicate stress, cardiovascular strain, illness, or abnormal physiological adaptation. Persistent values below 50 bpm or above 120 bpm require immediate evaluation.
heart_rate.actions: Recheck the measurement, reduce physical activity temporarily, review recent workload and stress levels and continue monitoring trends over time.
heart_rate.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if heart rate remains below 50 bpm or above 120 bpm, shows a persistent abnormal trend, or is accompanied by dizziness, weakness, chest discomfort, or impaired performance.

blood_pressure.title: Blood pressure
blood_pressure.howToMeasure: Blood pressure is measured using an automatic blood pressure monitor or medical-grade sphygmomanometer.
blood_pressure.whyItMatters: Blood pressure reflects how effectively the cardiovascular system delivers blood throughout the body. Abnormal blood pressure can indicate cardiovascular stress or impaired physiological adaptation.
blood_pressure.spaceRisk: Blood pressure reflects how effectively the cardiovascular system delivers blood throughout the body. Abnormal blood pressure can indicate cardiovascular stress or impaired physiological adaptation.
blood_pressure.whenToWorry: Blood pressure consistently in the attention range may indicate developing cardiovascular stress. Blood pressure in the critical range requires prompt assessment.
blood_pressure.actions: Repeat the measurement after a period of rest, review hydration status, evaluate workload and stress factors, monitor trends over time.
blood_pressure.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if systolic pressure reaches or exceeds 140 mmHg, diastolic pressure reaches or exceeds 90 mmHg, or if abnormal readings persist over multiple measurements.

body_temperature.title: Body temperature
body_temperature.howToMeasure: Body temperature, measured in degrees Celsius (°C), using a digital thermometer or continuous physiological monitoring system.
body_temperature.whyItMatters: Body temperature is a fundamental indicator of health. Changes may signal infection, inflammation, altered immune response, or physiological stress.
body_temperature.spaceRisk: Impacted by microgravity, radiation exposure, circadian rhythm disruption, and physiological stress can affect the immune system during spaceflight. Monitoring body temperature helps identify potential health issues that may affect crew performance.
body_temperature.whenToWorry: Temperatures outside the normal range or impaired thermoregulation or physiological stress is spotted. Fever or hypothermia requires immediate attention.
body_temperature.actions: Repeat the measurement, monitor for additional symptoms, reduce workload if necessary, increase monitoring frequency.
body_temperature.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if temperature reaches 38.0°C or higher, falls below 35.0°C, or is accompanied by signs of illness or reduced performance.

blood_glucose.title: Blood glucose
blood_glucose.howToMeasure: Blood glucose is measured using a glucose meter or continuous glucose monitoring system.
blood_glucose.whyItMatters: Blood glucose reflects how effectively the body regulates energy and metabolism. Maintaining stable glucose levels is important for cognitive performance, physical function, and overall health.
blood_glucose.spaceRisk: Spaceflight can affect insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion, and glucose metabolism. Monitoring glucose may help detect metabolic changes associated with long-duration missions.
blood_glucose.whenToWorry: Values above the normal range may indicate impaired glucose regulation. Values below 70 mg/dL may indicate hypoglycemia and require immediate attention.
blood_glucose.actions: Repeat the measurement, review recent food intake, assess workload and stress levels, continue monitoring trends.
blood_glucose.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if glucose falls below 70 mg/dL, rises to 126 mg/dL or higher, or remains abnormal over repeated measurements.

sleep.title: Sleep
sleep.howToMeasure: Sleep is measured as a total number of hours spent sleeping in 24-hour period. The data can be collected using a sleep tracker, wearable device or a daily sleep log.
sleep.whyItMatters: Good sleep is essential for performance, reaction time and decision-making as well as emotional stability and health. Poor sleep can reduce mission performance and increase the risk of errors. Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules.
sleep.spaceRisk: Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, irregular light-dark cycles, and work overload as significant risks during spaceflight.
sleep.whenToWorry: Sleep below 7 hours may indicate insufficient recovery. Sleep below 5 hours is considered critical and may negatively affect alertness, cognitive performance, and mission readiness.
sleep.actions: Review workload and daily schedule, maintain a consistent sleep routine, use designated rest periods and recovery time, and continue monitoring sleep duration over the next several days. Report persistent sleep difficulties to the medical team.
sleep.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if sleep remains below 5 hours for multiple days or if fatigue begins to affect performance, alertness, decision-making, or mood.

mood.title: Mood
mood.howToMeasure: Mood is measured using a self-reported score from 1 to 5, where 1 represents very poor mood and 5 represents excellent mood.
mood.whyItMatters: Mood provides a simple indicator of psychological well-being, stress levels, and adaptation to long-duration space missions. Bad mood can influence mission readiness.
mood.spaceRisk: Isolation, confinement, workload, interpersonal stress, and long-duration missions can negatively affect behavioral health and crew performance. Human Factors and Behavioral Performance.
mood.whenToWorry: A score of 3 may indicate elevated stress or reduced well-being. Scores of 1-2 may suggest significant psychological strain and require additional assessment.
mood.actions: Review workload and sources of stress, reschedule personal recovery or relaxation time, and continue monitoring mood trends over time. Seek behavioral health support if symptoms persist.
mood.callFlightSurgeon: Contact the Flight Surgeon if mood scores remain at 1-2, continue to decline over time, or begin affecting teamwork, daily activities, or mission performance.
